question: Light entering the eye is focused onto the retina mainly by:

options.text: The cornea and the lens acting together
The iris alone
The optic nerve
The fovea alone, with no other structure involved

explanation: The cornea provides most of the eye's fixed focusing power, and the lens makes the finer, adjustable adjustments (accommodation) needed to bring objects at different distances into sharp focus on the retina.

question: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye by:

options.text: Adjusting the diameter of the pupil
Changing the curvature of the cornea
Moving the retina closer to or further from the lens
Secreting tears

explanation: The iris is a muscular ring that widens or narrows the pupil at its centre, directly regulating how much light reaches the retina — much like the aperture of a camera.

question: The sharpest visual acuity occurs when light falls on:

options.text: The fovea, a small central area of the retina densely packed with cone cells
The blind spot
The peripheral retina, away from the centre
The cornea directly, without passing through the lens

explanation: The fovea is a small, cone-dense region at the centre of the retina specialised for fine detail and colour. Vision falls off in sharpness rapidly moving away from it toward the rod-dominated periphery.

question: Cone cells and rod cells in the retina differ mainly in that:

options.text: Cones provide colour vision and fine detail in good light, while rods provide monochrome vision that works in much dimmer light
Rods provide colour vision and cones provide only black-and-white vision
Both respond identically to light and colour
Cones are found only in the blind spot

explanation: Cones need relatively bright light but resolve colour and fine detail, concentrated at the fovea. Rods are far more sensitive to low light but cannot distinguish colour, and dominate the peripheral retina — which is why colour and detail are the first things lost as light fades.

question: Because the fovea contains almost no rod cells, a pilot scanning for a dim light or another aircraft at night should:

options.text: Look slightly off to one side of the object rather than directly at it, using peripheral (off-centre) vision
Stare directly at the object without moving the eyes
Close one eye to improve night vision
Rely on central vision, which is more sensitive at night

explanation: Looking straight at a faint object at night puts its image on the rod-poor fovea, where it may not register at all. Off-centre viewing shifts the image onto the rod-rich peripheral retina, which is far more sensitive in low light.

question: Full dark adaptation of the eye, allowing it to make the most of rod-based night vision, takes:

options.text: Up to around 30 minutes, much longer than the eye needs to adjust from dark back to bright light
Less than one second
Exactly the same time as adjusting from darkness to brightness
Several days

explanation: Rod sensitivity builds up gradually over many minutes in the dark, whereas the eye adapts back to bright light far faster. A single bright flash (cockpit light, a phone screen) can undo a long dark-adaptation process almost instantly.

question: Cabin and instrument lighting is often dimmed to a low red or subdued white level before a night flight mainly to:

options.text: Preserve the crew's dark adaptation while still allowing instruments to be read
Reduce electrical load on the aircraft's battery
Make the cabin look more comfortable for passengers
Improve colour vision at night

explanation: Keeping cockpit lighting low protects the rod-based dark adaptation the crew needs for the outside scene, while still providing enough light to read instruments — a balance that bright white lighting would defeat.

question: The eye's "blind spot" exists because:

options.text: The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye has no photoreceptor cells at all
The fovea contains no cone cells
The cornea is opaque at its centre
The lens blocks light from reaching one portion of the retina

explanation: Where the optic nerve exits the eye, there is a gap with no rods or cones, so any image falling exactly there cannot be detected. The brain normally fills in this gap unnoticed, using information from the other eye and from context.

question: The practical danger of the blind spot in a scan for other traffic is that:

options.text: A small, distant aircraft could, by coincidence, fall exactly on the blind spot of a stationary eye and go completely undetected
It only affects peripheral vision, never anything near the centre of the visual field
It is present in only one eye out of every ten people
It disappears completely once dark adaptation is achieved

explanation: Because the blind spot is a true gap in the retina, a small, unmoving target at just the wrong angle can vanish from a fixed gaze entirely. A moving, scanning search pattern, rather than a single fixed stare, helps ensure nothing stays hidden there for long.

question: Stereoscopic vision (depth perception from comparing the slightly different images from both eyes) is most useful for judging distance:

options.text: At relatively close range, becoming far less effective as distance increases
At very long range, such as judging the distance to another aircraft many miles away
Equally well at all distances, with no limit
Only in complete darkness

explanation: Stereopsis depends on the small difference between the two eyes' viewpoints, which becomes negligible once an object is far enough away. At the distances relevant to most collision-avoidance scanning, a pilot relies on monocular cues — relative size, motion, perspective — rather than stereopsis.

question: "Empty-field myopia" refers to the tendency of the eye, when there is no object to focus on (such as a featureless sky or haze), to:

options.text: Relax to a near resting focus distance, so a distant object entering that empty field may not be sharply focused, or even consciously registered, straight away
Focus automatically at infinity, giving the sharpest possible distance vision
Lose the ability to focus on anything at all
Only occur to pilots wearing glasses

explanation: Without a visual target to lock onto, the eye's focusing muscles relax toward a comfortable near distance rather than infinity. A distant aircraft appearing in otherwise empty sky can therefore take a moment to be sharply resolved, which is relevant to how quickly conflicting traffic is actually seen.

question: A practical countermeasure for empty-field myopia during a visual traffic scan is to:

options.text: Deliberately refocus on something at a known distance, such as a wingtip, periodically during the scan
Stare fixedly at the horizon without moving the eyes
Close one eye for the duration of the scan
Reduce airspeed to zero

explanation: Giving the eyes an occasional near object to focus on resets accommodation away from the resting near-point default, helping ensure the eyes are actually focused for distance when scanning featureless sky, rather than relaxed at a short, blurry distance.

question: A pilot who can see distant objects clearly but struggles to focus on close objects (such as instruments or charts) most likely has:

options.text: Hyperopia (long-sightedness)
Myopia (short-sightedness)
Colour blindness
A permanent blind spot enlargement

explanation: Hyperopia means light focuses behind the retina for near objects, making close work blurry while distance vision remains relatively clear — the opposite pattern to myopia, where distant objects are blurred and close objects are clear.

question: Presbyopia, the gradual loss of the eye's ability to focus on near objects with age, occurs mainly because:

options.text: The lens becomes progressively less flexible, reducing its ability to change shape (accommodate) for close focus
The cornea becomes more curved with age
The number of cone cells doubles with age
The retina detaches progressively over decades

explanation: The lens stiffens with age, reducing the range of accommodation available for near focus. This is why many pilots, with no other visual defect, find they need reading glasses for charts and instruments as they get older even though their distance vision stays good.

question: A pilot considering contact lenses rather than spectacles should be aware that:

options.text: Appropriate lens type and good ocular health matter, since reduced tear flow, dry cockpit air or a poorly fitted lens can cause discomfort or blurred vision at an inconvenient time
Contact lenses eliminate the need for any aeromedical consideration whatsoever
All types of contact lenses behave identically in every environment
Contact lenses are never permitted for any flying duties

explanation: The low-humidity cockpit environment can dry the eyes, and lens type and fit matter for comfort and reliable vision over a long flight — considerations that make the choice an aeromedical one, not simply a matter of personal convenience.

question: Colour vision is produced by three types of cone cell, each most sensitive to a different range of wavelengths. Red-green colour blindness most commonly results from:

options.text: A deficiency or anomaly in one of the cone types responsible for distinguishing red and green wavelengths
A complete absence of all three cone types
Damage to the rod cells only
A problem with the cornea rather than the retina

explanation: The most common forms of colour blindness involve one of the red- or green-sensitive cone types being missing or shifted in sensitivity, making red and green hues harder to distinguish, while the blue-sensitive cones and overall brightness perception are unaffected.

question: Colour vision deficiency is operationally significant for a pilot mainly because:

options.text: Several safety-critical cues — navigation light colours, signal lamps, some chart symbology — rely on correctly distinguishing colour
It prevents a person from reading any text at all
It only affects vision in complete darkness
It has no bearing on flying and is purely cosmetic

explanation: Aviation deliberately encodes some safety information in colour — navigation lights, light-gun signals, certain instrument and chart cues — so a colour vision deficiency can affect a pilot's ability to interpret those cues correctly, which is why it is assessed as part of the medical examination.

question: The difficulty of visually detecting another aircraft on a near-collision course, despite "see and avoid", is explained partly by the fact that:

options.text: An aircraft closing on a constant collision course shows almost no relative movement in the windscreen, growing only slowly in apparent size until very late
Approaching aircraft always move rapidly across the field of view, making them easy to spot
The visual system can process closure rates of any speed with no delay
Collision geometry only matters for aircraft of very different speeds

explanation: An object truly on a collision course presents a constant bearing and barely changing size for most of the time before impact — exactly the condition the eye is worst at detecting, since it relies heavily on relative motion to notice something new in a visual field.

question: An effective visual scanning technique for detecting traffic is generally based on:

options.text: Short, overlapping segments of the sky with brief pauses to fixate, rather than one continuous sweeping motion
One continuous, smooth sweep across the entire horizon without pausing
Looking only straight ahead, since peripheral vision contributes nothing useful
Scanning as fast as physically possible to cover more sky per second

explanation: The eye needs a brief pause to resolve detail; a continuous smooth sweep blurs everything and resolves nothing properly. Scanning in short segments with momentary fixations gives the visual system the stationary moments it needs to actually detect something small and distant.

question: A pilot who has lost the use of one eye can usually still fly safely for most purposes mainly because:

options.text: Most distance judgement in flying relies on monocular cues (relative size, motion, perspective) rather than on binocular stereopsis
Binocular vision contributes nothing useful to flying in the first place
One eye automatically compensates by doubling its resolution
Depth perception is entirely unaffected by losing an eye

explanation: Because stereopsis is only useful at close range in any case, losing it does not remove the dominant cues — size, parallax from head movement, perspective — that a pilot actually relies on for distance and depth judgement in the air, though the loss of visual field and some near-range depth perception still matters.

question: Good quality sunglasses are recommended for flying mainly because they:

options.text: Reduce glare and bright-light discomfort without distorting colour perception or blocking light needed to read instruments or signals
Improve night vision when worn after dark
Eliminate the need for dark adaptation entirely
Are only a cosmetic accessory with no visual benefit

explanation: The right sunglasses cut uncomfortable glare and reduce squinting fatigue while preserving accurate colour and enough light transmission to read cockpit displays or external signals — poorly chosen tints or polarization can interfere with exactly those needs.

question: Saccades — the rapid, jerky movements the eye makes when scanning a scene — are significant for a pilot because:

options.text: Vision is effectively suspended for a brief moment during each saccade, so information is only gathered during the pauses between them
They allow continuous, uninterrupted vision throughout the movement
They only occur while the eyes are closed
They have no bearing on instrument scanning

explanation: The visual system suppresses input during the rapid jump itself to avoid a blurred image, so useful information is actually gathered during the brief fixations between saccades — which is part of why an efficient, disciplined instrument scan matters more than simply moving the eyes quickly.
